newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Masood deals heavy blow to Afghan Taleban.
newsitem.headline: Masood deals heavy blow to Afghan Taleban.

text.p: Men loyal to former Afghan military chief Ahmad Shah Masood had cut off a large Taleban militia force in the narrow Salang Pass on Wednesday and inflicted heavy casualties, Western aid workers said.

The counter-attack was directed by Basir Solangi, Masood's commander in the Salang Pass who withdrew north into territory controlled by Uzbek leader Abdul Rashid Dostum as the Islamic militia pushed up from Kabul.

The attack had forced the Taleban to call off, at least temporarily, their attempt to battle their way into Masood's Panjsher valley stronghold from the town of Golbahar, which sits astride the sheer-sided gorge that leads into it.
"There are no Taleban left in Golbahar," said one aid worker quoting witnesses.
There was no independent confirmation of the report. Taleban fighters turned back western journalists just south of Jabal-os-Siraj, the regional Taleban headquarters.
Usually happy to chat about what is going on at the front, the fighters said they had no information.

The attack by a Masood commander who only last week was described by an Uzbek general as Dostum's "honoured guest" appeared to bring closer a formal alliance between Masood and the Uzbek leader against the Taleban.

On Tuesday, Dostum publicly embraced Burhanuddin Rabbani, president of the ousted government, and told reporters in his city of Mazar-i-Sharif, 400 km (250 miles) northwest of Kabul, that Masood was expected there on Wednesday or Thursday.

The road to Golbahar leaves the Salang highway at Jabal-os-Siraj. Between the Panjsher and the pass are a series of high ridges and only Masood's native Tajiks are thought to know routes across them. Taleban fighters said Solangi's attack came through the pass and over the mountains.
The western aid workers said the Taleban, mostly ethnic Pushtuns from southern Afghanistan, had lost around 270 men in their assault into the ethnic Tajik Panjsher since Saturday.
They said many of the casualties had been caused by mines at the entrance to the gorge and on the slim road, across which Masood's men brought down landslides to seal the gorge.
Taleban losses in Solangi's counter-attack were even more severe in fighting that began on Tuesday morning, the aid workers said.
They said witnesses counted at least 100 dead Taleban being brought down the Salang Highway to Jabal-os-Siraj. "One counted 39 bodies being brought down in just one hour," one said.

They said many more Taleban had been injured in Solangi's attack, which began with his men cutting the road behind forward Taleban positions and isolating a large number of the black-turbanned warriors.

Solangi, a local man who destroyed a Soviet battalion in the pass when Moscow backed a communist government in Kabul in the 1980s, controlled the mountaintops almost all the way down to Jabal-os-Siraj, they said.

The sources said the Taleban had sent tanks, multiple rocket launchers, anti-aircraft guns and scores of jeeps loaded with fighters up the Salang highway, but that they had come under heavy artillery fire from Solangi's guns.

Dostum moved armour and men south of the Salang Tunnel, a key choke point on the road from Kabul to Mazar-i-Sharif, as the Taleban took the Afghan capital and said on Sunday he would back those opposed to the Taleban if the militia did not stop fighting.

A new alliance between Masood and Dostum -- a previous one shattered in 1994 and the Uzbek chief withdrew to the north where he controls six of Afghanistan's 33 provinces -- would be a major problem for the Taleban, who have imposed the strict Islamic Sharia law wherever they have taken control.

They have swept all before them since the movement was born in religious schools in refugee camps in Pakistan, but now are facing one very tough opponent in Masood and could be confronting another in Dostum.
Dostum favours a liberal interpretation of Islam. His men often drink, an abhorrence to the Taleban, and are among the toughest fighters in a land of tough fighters.
